summary: A scholar in sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and history/archaeology, Franke studied at Cologne, Bonn, and Berlin under Erich Haenisch. He served as professor at the University of Munich (~1952–1979) and president of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences (~1980–1985).

Specializing in Indology, history/archaeology, and Buddhist studies, Härtel studied under Ernst Waldschmidt (~1946–1953). He served as director of the Museum für Asiatische Kunst (~1963–1986) and professor at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1965–1986).
Active in Indology and philosophy, Randle served as librarian at both the India Office and the India Office Library from approximately 1933 to 1946.

Guenther worked in Buddhist studies, Tibetology, and philosophy. He studied at the University of Saskatchewan and under several traditional teachers, including Tarthang Tulku. He was a professor at the University of Saskatchewan (~1964–1984) and taught scholars including Leonard van der Kuijp.

A linguist, Smyth studied at Swarthmore, Harvard, Leipzig, and Göttingen. He held academic posts at Williams College (~1883–1885), Johns Hopkins (~1885–1888), Bryn Mawr (~1888–1901), and Harvard University (~1901–1925).

Kellgren worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied under Hermann Brockhaus (~1845–1846), Eugène Burnouf (~1846–1849), and Philippe-Édouard Foucaux (~1846–1849), later holding a post at the University of Helsinki (~1849–1856).
Specializing in Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies, Beckh studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1903–1907) and subsequently held an academic post there from approximately 1908 to 1921.
Beythan was a scholar in Indology and linguistics who studied under the traditional teachers Ramasami Aiyar and Radscha Pillai.

Brockhaus studied at Leipzig and under August Wilhelm Schlegel before holding professorships at Jena (1839–1841) and Leipzig (1848–1877). Working in Indology, linguistics, and Iranian/Central Asian studies, he founded the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft and taught Friedrich Max Müller.

An Indologist who studied under Albrecht Weber, Brunnhofer succeeded Franz Kielhorn in 1866. He later taught at Goldingen Gymnasium (1889) and served as titular professor at the University of Bern (1901–1914).
An Indologist, Kellner studied under Hermann Brockhaus and served as Gymnasialprofessor at the Gymnasium zu Zwickau.

A linguist and Indologist, Collitz studied at Johanneum Lüneburg and Göttingen under Theodor Benfey. He held posts as professor at Bryn Mawr College (1885–1907) and professor of Germanic philology at Johns Hopkins University (1907–1930).

Goetz worked in Indology and history/archaeology, having studied at the University of Munich (~1920–1924). He served as curator at the Baroda Museum and Picture Gallery (~1940–1953) and held a post at Heidelberg University (~1961–1976).

A scholar of Indology and linguistics, Grassmann studied at Frederick William University Berlin and under Rudolf von Roth. He held posts at Gewerbeschule and Friedrich-Wilhelms-Gymnasium, and served as professor at Marienstiftsgymnasium Stettin (1832–1877).

Hirt worked in linguistics and Indology, completing studies at the universities of Freiburg (~1886–1888) and Leipzig (~1888–1890). He later held academic posts at Leipzig University (~1896–1912) and the University of Giessen (~1912–1935).

Jacobi was an Indologist and linguist who studied in Berlin, Bonn, and Calcutta. He held posts at Münster, Kiel, and the University of Bonn (~1889–1921), as well as Munich and Cologne, teaching students such as Helmuth von Glasenapp.

A scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology, Kulke completed his PhD at the University of Freiburg (~1961–1967). He held a post at Heidelberg University (~1967–1988) and the Chair of Asian History at the University of Kiel (1988).

Oldenberg worked in Indology and Buddhist studies after studying at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1871–1875). He held posts at Berlin (1888), Kiel (~1889–1901), and Göttingen (~1904–1920), teaching scholars including Ferdinand de Saussure.
A linguist and Indologist, Osthoff co-founded Morphologische Untersuchungen. He held academic posts at Leipzig University (~1875–1877) and Heidelberg University (~1877–1909).
Sauppe was a scholar in linguistics and history/archaeology. He held academic positions at the University of Zurich (~1838–1845) and the University of Göttingen (~1856–1893), and taught Georg Bühler.
